title: Deep inelastic scattering as a probe of entanglement: the complete QCD dipole cascade
authors: Martin Hentschinski, Krzysztof Kutak, Wieslaw Placzek, Martin Rohrmoser
abstract: We study entanglement entropy in Deep Inelastic Scattering (DIS) using the dipole formulation of the high-energy limit of QCD. We argue that a reduced density matrix arises in low $x$ DIS due to a trace over unobserved color degrees of freedom and we obtain entanglement entropy in terms of dipole multiplicities, directly from the von Neumann entropy.   %In the present study we explicitly construct a density matrix representing the entangled state of the photon and proton and perform a trace over unobserved degrees of freedom. Dipole multiplicities are obtained from a solution to low $x$ evolution equations, which we solve numerically. Unlike previous studies, we take into account both transverse-size and azimuthal-angle dependence in the dipole evolution kernel. We study both the exact solution of the equation as well as its double leading-logarithmic approximation (DLLA). We find that for the same initial dipole size, the DLLA solution generates a larger entropy. %We interpret this as information loss due to erasing data on daughter dipole sizes. Finally, we calculate the dipole multiplicities and entanglement entropy and compare our results to the Shannon entropy of hadron multiplicities, as measured by the H1 collaboration.
summary: This paper applies concepts from quantum information theory to Deep Inelastic Scattering (DIS) within the framework of high-energy QCD dipoles. It calculates the entanglement entropy by analyzing how tracing over unobserved color degrees of freedom affects the system's density matrix. The results provide a theoretical prediction for entanglement in hadronic structure, comparing it against experimental measurements.
main_problem: The study investigates how entanglement entropy can be calculated in Deep Inelastic Scattering (DIS) by treating the process using the dipole formulation of high-energy Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). The goal is to quantify information loss due to tracing over unobserved color degrees of freedom.
main_result: The authors derive entanglement entropy directly from von Neumann entropy using dipole multiplicities, finding that the Double Leading Logarithmic Approximation (DLLA) yields a larger entropy compared to other methods for the same initial conditions. These results are compared against empirical measurements from the H1 collaboration.
method: The methodology involves deriving the reduced density matrix by tracing over unobserved color degrees of freedom and solving low-$x$ evolution equations governing dipole multiplicities, considering both transverse-size and azimuthal-angle dependence.
model_or_system: The physical system is DIS ($	ext{electron} + 	ext{proton}$), modeled using the QCD dipole formulation in the high-energy limit. The theoretical framework relies on solving generalized BFKL-type evolution equations for color dipoles, leading to a description of the proton as an entangled quantum state.
key_observables: Entanglement entropy ($S$), dipole multiplicities ($\langle n angle$), and comparison with Shannon entropy measured by the H1 collaboration.
important_parameters: Low Bjorken $x$, transverse size, azimuthal angle dependence, and the evolution scale $Q^2$.
main_assumptions: The derivation assumes that a reduced density matrix accurately describes the system after tracing over unobserved degrees of freedom. Approximations include using DLLA and assuming high-energy factorization.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically illustrates the scattering process involving two color dipoles, demonstrating coherence loss as the color charge is modified during the interaction.
paper_structure: The paper develops from establishing the formalism of entanglement entropy in DIS using the dipole basis to solving the relevant low-$x$ evolution equations (including DLLA) and finally comparing the calculated entropy with existing experimental data.
why_interesting: While focused on QCD, the core mathematical machinery—calculating entanglement entropy from reduced density matrices derived from complex field theory dynamics—is highly relevant to open quantum systems and many-body physics simulations.
